summary: on SQLite a statement whose source query is a compound SELECT (UNION, EXCEPT, INTERSECT, not UNION ALL) loses its outer statement: the inspector reports a plain select over one branch, so the write is never checked and the other branches are never named
scenario: an analyst holding only select on other.t3 writes rows into main.t1 with INSERT INTO t1 (c1) SELECT c1 FROM t2 UNION SELECT c1 FROM other.t3, and with a constant last branch the deny-all policy allows the statement outright, so a principal holding no grant at all inserts rows
defence: the merge in dialect/sqlite/inspect.go exists to repair a parser artifact, since ANTLR splits A UNION B into adjacent sql_stmt_list nodes and without it even SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 2 reports as two statements, so this could be read as the known unreadable-branch-degrades-to-nothing class scoped to one dialect. It does not hold: the insert_stmt branch parses cleanly and is then discarded, so the result is not an empty read but a write relabelled as a read, which defeats the UnknownStatement floor by construction; PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite with UNION ALL all get it right

summary: WITH before INSERT on the MySQL dialect floors to unknown statements and asks for manage, so no right on the insert target is ever checked
scenario: no realistic one: MySQL rejects WITH ... INSERT with a syntax error, so no statement runs and no row is touched
defence: MySQL permits WITH at the head of SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE and immediately before the SELECT of an INSERT ... SELECT, and nowhere else; MySQLParser.g4 carries withClause on deleteStatement, queryExpression and updateStatement but not on insertStatement. The cases are the one spelling the server refuses, so the unknown-statement floor is the designed answer and the refusal costs a data role nothing. The defence holds; the cases were rewritten as skips and the expectation was wrong. The residue is a diagnosis quality defect at most: the user is told they lack manage when the truth is a syntax error

summary: PostgreSQL MERGE floors to an unknown statement and asks only for manage, so neither the update on the target nor the reads of the source are checked
scenario: an operator holding manage but no insert or update right runs MERGE INTO t1 USING t2 ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET c2 = b.c3 and rewrites rows of main.t1, while an analyst holding the four data actions is refused a statement they should be allowed
defence: not reviewed adversarially this run; the unknown-statement floor is documented behaviour for a statement the inspector does not dispatch on, and MERGE may simply be unsupported on purpose

summary: the alias of a target in a MySQL multi-table DELETE list is linted as an unknown table, and the alias of the second table of a multi-table UPDATE list does not resolve its columns, so valid MySQL is marked with unknown-table and unknown-column warnings
scenario: a MySQL user writes the ordinary join-delete DELETE a FROM t1 AS a JOIN t2 ON a.c1 = t2.c1 or the join-update UPDATE t1 AS a, t2 AS b SET a.c2 = 'x' WHERE a.c1 = b.c1; both are valid and both get the right permission verdict, but the editor warns unknown table or view 'a' and unknown column 'c1', so the user either learns to ignore the two rules most worth trusting or rewrites correct SQL to silence them
defence: the authoritative permission layer is right in all six cases, so nothing is over-granted or under-granted and what remains is a severity warning marker that blocks nothing; analyze_unknown_tables in lint_rules/references.py:32 walks every exp.Table, sqlglot's MySQL parse puts the pre-FROM target there, the rule has no alias-binding context at that point, and it does catch the real typo DELETE aa FROM t1 AS a. It does not hold: a warning that fires on valid SQL is the false positive class that teaches users to ignore the rule, and DELETE t1 FROM t1 JOIN t2 lints clean only because a table named t1 exists, so the rule is not distinguishing an alias from a table, it is looking the name up in the catalog. The review is right that there are two code sites, so the fix is two changes: alias scope for the DELETE target list, and a sources that covers the whole MySQL table reference list rather than args[from_] alone
